name: Daridorexant

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles daridorexant is discussed as an orexin-blocking prescription sleep drug (Quviviq), on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for insomnia; no appearance research exists.

summary: A prescription orexin-blocking insomnia drug (Quviviq); no appearance research exists.
note: Schedule IV in the US; label warns of next-day impairment and complex sleep behaviors.
currentQuick:
Daridorexant (Quviviq) is a prescription sleep medicine from the orexin-antagonist class, approved for adults with insomnia.
It has not been studied for any appearance outcome; any looksmaxxing relevance is through sleep and recovery in general.
How it works: It blocks orexin receptors OX1R and OX2R, dampening the brain's wake signal instead of enhancing GABA.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include sleepiness and headache; the label warns about next-day impairment, sleep paralysis, complex sleep behaviors and mood effects. It is prescription-only and Schedule IV in the US.
deepLead:
Daridorexant, sold as Quviviq, is a prescription dual orexin receptor antagonist for adults with insomnia involving difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep. It was developed by Idorsia Pharmaceuticals and was formerly known as nemorexant during development.
Grokipedia reports FDA approval on 7 January 2022 and European Medicines Agency approval on 29 April 2022, making it the third orexin receptor antagonist approved for insomnia after suvorexant and lemborexant. Two phase 3 trials examined both night-time and daytime symptoms of insomnia.
It has no approved or studied appearance indication. Its connection to looksmaxxing is limited to general conversation about sleep and recovery. Reported adverse effects include somnolence and headache, and the label warns of next-day impairment and complex sleep behaviors.

name: Eszopiclone

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles eszopiclone is discussed as a prescription Z-drug sleeping pill (Lunesta), on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for insomnia; appearance has not been studied.

summary: A prescription Z-drug sleeping pill (Lunesta); sleep research only, nothing on appearance.
note: Boxed FDA warning for complex sleep behaviors; Schedule IV.
currentQuick:
Eszopiclone (Lunesta) is a prescription Z-drug for insomnia, the active half of zopiclone.
It has not been studied for appearance; the only link is the general role of sleep in recovery.
How it works: It enhances GABA-A receptor signalling near the benzodiazepine site, producing sedation.
Risks and caveats: The FDA boxed warning covers complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking and sleep-driving; other reported effects include next-day impairment, dependence and mood changes. It is Schedule IV.
deepLead:
Eszopiclone, sold as Lunesta and as generics, is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the cyclopyrrolone class. It is the active (S)-enantiomer of zopiclone and is used for insomnia in adults.
The FDA approved it in December 2004. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US, and the FDA added a boxed warning in 2019 about serious injuries from complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking.
Eszopiclone has no approved appearance use and no published studies of appearance outcomes. It is mentioned here as part of the sleep-medicine landscape that some people connect with recovery.

name: Zaleplon

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles zaleplon is discussed as a short-acting prescription Z-drug for falling asleep, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for insomnia; appearance data do not exist.

summary: A short-acting prescription Z-drug sleeping pill (Sonata); no appearance data.
note: Schedule IV; complex sleep behaviors and dependence are labelled risks.
currentQuick:
Zaleplon (Sonata) is a prescription sleep medicine for short-term insomnia, notable for its roughly one-hour half-life.
It has not been studied for appearance.
How it works: It binds the BZ1 site on the GABA-A receptor, enhancing inhibitory signalling to induce sleep.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include headache, dizziness, sleepiness, amnesia and complex sleep behaviors; dependence can occur with prolonged use. Schedule IV in the US.
deepLead:
Zaleplon, sold as Sonata, is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic (pyrazolopyrimidine class) approved for short-term treatment of insomnia, particularly difficulty falling asleep.
It acts at the BZ1 site of the GABA-A receptor and has a very short half-life of about one hour, which Grokipedia says reduces next-day effects. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.
It has no approved or studied appearance use. Its inclusion in this wiki reflects its place among sleep medicines discussed in recovery contexts.

name: Zopiclone

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles zopiclone is discussed as a prescription Z-drug sleeping pill, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Some forum posters claim sleeping pills lower sleep quality over time; it is studied for insomnia, and appearance has not been studied.

summary: A prescription Z-drug sleeping pill (Imovane); not US-approved and untested for looks.
note: Dependence and tolerance risks; not approved in the US.
currentQuick:
Zopiclone is a prescription sleeping pill used in Europe, Canada and elsewhere for short-term severe insomnia.
It has not been tested for appearance; forum mentions are about sleep.
How it works: It enhances GABA-A receptor signalling at the benzodiazepine site, causing sedation.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include drowsiness, bitter taste, amnesia, behavioural changes, tolerance and dependence; treatment is usually limited to about four weeks.
deepLead:
Zopiclone is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the cyclopyrrolone class used for short-term treatment of severe insomnia in adults. It acts at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor.
Grokipedia reports it was first patented in 1972 and marketed from 1986 by Rhone-Poulenc under names such as Imovane and Zimovane; it is not approved in the United States, where its (S)-enantiomer eszopiclone is used.
It has no appearance indication. On looksmax.org it appears in occasional threads about sleep aids.

name: Temazepam

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles temazepam is discussed as a prescription benzodiazepine for short-term insomnia, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for sleep; appearance has not been studied.

summary: A prescription benzodiazepine sleeping pill; sleep research only, no appearance data.
note: Schedule IV; dependence risk, dangerous with opioids or alcohol.
currentQuick:
Temazepam is a prescription benzodiazepine used for short-term insomnia.
No research links it to appearance outcomes.
How it works: It enhances the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA at GABA-A receptors, causing sedation.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include drowsiness, amnesia, tolerance, dependence and withdrawal, and serious respiratory depression when combined with opioids or alcohol. Schedule IV in the US.
deepLead:
Temazepam is a short-to-intermediate-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic prescribed for short-term treatment of insomnia. It enhances GABA-A receptor activity, producing sedation, and is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.
Grokipedia reports it was synthesised in the 1960s and marketed internationally from the 1970s. It has no appearance indication and no studies of appearance outcomes.

name: Gabapentin

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles gabapentin is discussed as an off-label sleep aid, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is proven for nerve pain and seizures, and its looks effects are untested.

summary: A prescription nerve-pain and seizure drug that some people take off-label for sleep; proven for neuropathic pain, untested for looks.
note: Prescription-only; sedation, dizziness and misuse risk, especially with opioids or sedatives.
currentQuick:
Gabapentin is a prescription anticonvulsant approved in the US for postherpetic neuralgia and as add-on therapy for partial seizures. It is also prescribed off-label for many other conditions.
In looksmaxxing and recovery circles it is discussed as a possible sleep or anxiety aid. No published trial has tested it for appearance, and evidence for psychiatric use is described as limited.
How it works: It binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, which reduces release of excitatory neurotransmitters. Despite resembling GABA, it does not act on GABA binding, according to its label; the exact mechanism is unknown.
Risks and caveats: The label lists dizziness, somnolence and driving impairment, plus rare serious hypersensitivity reactions. Reference sources report misuse potential, especially combined with opioids or benzodiazepines. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Gabapentin is a prescription anticonvulsant and analgesic that is structurally related to the neurotransmitter GABA but, according to its US label, has no effect on GABA binding, uptake or degradation. It is sold under brand names including Neurontin and Gralise . The US label lists management of postherpetic neuralgia and adjunctive treatment of partial-onset seizures as its approved uses .
In looksmaxxing and recovery discussions it appears mainly as a drug taken off-label for sleep or anxiety. Published trials have mostly examined it in neuropathic pain, restless legs syndrome and epilepsy; no published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes, and evidence for sleep and anxiety use outside those conditions is described as limited in the reference literature .
Reference sources describe dizziness and somnolence as common adverse effects, and note misuse potential, particularly alongside opioids or sedatives. Its US controlled-substance status is unscheduled at the federal level, although some jurisdictions impose additional controls .

name: Pregabalin

angle.text: Forum posters take pregabalin to lower social anxiety and inhibition, hoping to come across as more relaxed and confident. It is approved for nerve pain, fibromyalgia and seizures; that social use is untested.

summary: A prescription nerve-pain and anxiety-adjacent drug that forum users take to lower social inhibition; untested for that use and carries misuse and withdrawal risks.
note: Controlled substance (US Schedule V); withdrawal warnings on label.
currentQuick:
Pregabalin (Lyrica) is a prescription gabapentinoid approved for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia and add-on seizure treatment, and licensed for generalized anxiety disorder in some regions.
On looksmax.org, users describe taking it to feel less inhibited in social situations. These are anecdotes; no trial has tested it for that goal in healthy people.
How it works: It binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate, although the precise mechanism is not fully established.
Risks and caveats: The label warns of respiratory depression with other CNS depressants, suicidal thoughts, angioedema, dizziness, somnolence, peripheral edema, weight gain and withdrawal reactions. It is a Schedule V drug in the US, and reference sources note misuse potential.
deepLead:
Pregabalin is a prescription gabapentinoid, structurally related to GABA, sold by Pfizer as Lyrica. The US label lists diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, fibromyalgia, spinal-cord-injury neuropathic pain and adjunctive treatment of partial-onset seizures .
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed mainly as a social-disinhibition or anxiety-relief drug; users on looksmax.org have described taking it before social situations and have exchanged questions about obtaining it and about withdrawal . These accounts are anecdotal, and no published trial has tested pregabalin for this purpose in people without a diagnosed condition.
Grokipedia reports that pregabalin is a Schedule V controlled substance in the US and that its euphoric and sedative effects at high amounts have led to concerns about misuse . The label warns of respiratory depression with other CNS depressants, suicidal ideation, angioedema and withdrawal effects after abrupt discontinuation .

name: Mirtazapine

angle.text: Mirtazapine is used off-label for sleep, and some users, such as those trying to gain weight, value its appetite boost. It is approved for depression; its effects on looks are untested.

summary: A sedating, appetite-boosting prescription antidepressant sometimes used off-label for sleep; approved for depression, untested for looks.
note: Boxed warning for suicidality in young people; weight gain and heavy sedation are common.
currentQuick:
Mirtazapine is a prescription antidepressant approved in the US for major depressive disorder in adults. Its sedating and appetite-increasing effects lead to off-label use for insomnia and appetite loss.
No published trial has tested it for appearance goals, and the wiki found no community discussion to cite.
How it works: It is thought to block presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, raising noradrenergic and serotonergic activity, and also blocks several serotonin receptors and histamine H1, which is linked to sedation.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include drowsiness, weight gain, dry mouth, constipation and raised cholesterol. The label has a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts in young people and lists agranulocytosis, serotonin syndrome and QT prolongation. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Mirtazapine is a tetracyclic antidepressant, classed as a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant, sold as Remeron. The US label lists major depressive disorder in adults as its indication .
It is discussed in sleep and recovery contexts because it is sedating and increases appetite; off-label uses reported in reference sources include insomnia, PTSD, anxiety disorders and appetite stimulation in medical illness . No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes, and the wiki found no community threads about it that could be cited.
The label carries a boxed warning about suicidal thoughts and behaviors in young people and lists agranulocytosis, serotonin syndrome, angle-closure glaucoma and QT prolongation among warnings .

name: Sodium oxybate (GHB)

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles sodium oxybate is discussed as a prescription drug that deepens slow-wave sleep, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is approved for narcolepsy; use for looks is untested.

summary: A narcolepsy prescription drug that is chemically GHB; approved for sleep disorders, untested for looks, and tightly controlled for serious safety reasons.
note: Boxed warning for CNS depression and abuse; restricted distribution and controlled-substance status.
currentQuick:
Sodium oxybate is the prescription form of GHB, approved in the US for cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy. It is tightly controlled.
It appears in recovery and sleep discussions because it deepens slow-wave sleep. No trial has tested it for appearance outcomes, and the wiki found no community threads to cite.
How it works: It acts at GABA-B receptors and GHB-specific receptors, depressing the central nervous system and increasing slow-wave sleep.
Risks and caveats: The label boxed warning covers CNS and respiratory depression and abuse or misuse. Reference sources report overdose risk, especially with alcohol or sedatives. It is a controlled substance, with restricted distribution as a medicine.
deepLead:
Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a central nervous system depressant. As a prescription product it is approved in the US for cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy . The same compound is also a controlled drug outside medical use.
It is listed in recovery and sleep discussions because of its reported effect on slow-wave sleep . No published trial has examined it for looksmaxxing outcomes, and the wiki found no community threads that could be cited.
The US label carries a boxed warning for central nervous system depression and for abuse and misuse . Grokipedia reports it is a Schedule III drug when marketed for narcolepsy, with restricted distribution programs .

name: Prazosin

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles prazosin is discussed as an off-label option for trauma-related nightmares that disrupt sleep, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for blood pressure and PTSD nightmares; nothing links it to appearance.

summary: A blood-pressure alpha-blocker used off-label for trauma nightmares; nothing connects it to appearance.
note: Fainting and low blood pressure, especially after the first dose.
currentQuick:
Prazosin is a prescription alpha-1 blocker approved for high blood pressure. Clinicians also use it off-label for benign prostatic hyperplasia and for nightmares linked to PTSD.
No trial has tested it for looks, and the wiki found no community discussion to cite.
How it works: It blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, relaxing blood vessels and, for nightmares, dampening noradrenergic activity during sleep according to reference sources.
Risks and caveats: The label lists dizziness, headache, drowsiness and weakness, and warns of fainting from postural low blood pressure, notably with the first dose. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Prazosin is an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blocker. The US label lists hypertension as its indication . Reference sources describe off-label use for benign prostatic hyperplasia, Raynaud's phenomenon and nightmares associated with post-traumatic stress disorder .
It is included in this wiki because of its use for trauma-related nightmares and sleep disturbance. No published trial has tested prazosin for appearance outcomes, and the wiki found no community threads about it that could be cited.
Common adverse effects on the label include dizziness, headache and drowsiness, and the label warns of syncope with sudden loss of consciousness, often linked to postural hypotension .

name: Clonidine

angle.text: Forum posters include clonidine in stress stacks, alongside pregnenolone and cyproheptadine, aiming for lower stress, calmer nights and a more rested look. It is a prescription blood-pressure and ADHD drug; its use for appearance is anecdotal and has not been tested.

summary: A blood-pressure and ADHD prescription drug that surfaces in forum stress stacks; nothing tests it for looks.
note: Rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly; dry mouth, drowsiness and low blood pressure are common.
currentQuick:
Clonidine is a prescription alpha-2 agonist used for high blood pressure, and in extended-release form for ADHD in children and adolescents.
On looksmax.org one thread reposts a suggestion to combine it with pregnenolone and cyproheptadine for stress. No published study has tested that.
How it works: It activates alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, lowering sympathetic nervous system output, heart rate and vascular resistance.
Risks and caveats: The label reports dry mouth, drowsiness, dizziness and constipation, and warns that abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound high blood pressure. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Clonidine is a centrally acting alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. The US label for the tablets lists hypertension as the indication . Extended-release forms are approved for ADHD in children and adolescents .
In looksmaxxing-adjacent forums it appears in discussions of stress, sleep and 'dopamine' protocols; one looksmax.org thread reposts a forum user's suggestion to combine pregnenolone, clonidine and cyproheptadine for stress and attention problems . No published trial has tested such a combination or clonidine for appearance outcomes.
Common adverse effects on the label include dry mouth, drowsiness and dizziness, and the label warns against abrupt discontinuation because of rebound hypertension .

name: Zuranolone

angle.text: Zuranolone is an approved postpartum depression drug that occasionally comes up in neurosteroid and mood-recovery discussions. Any appearance link runs through mood and sleep improvement; it has been studied for depression only, not for looks.

summary: Prescription oral neurosteroid approved for postpartum depression; not an appearance compound, and carries a driving-impairment boxed warning.
note: Schedule IV in the US with a boxed warning on driving impairment.
currentQuick:
Zuranolone is a prescription capsule taken as a 14-day course for postpartum depression. It is a lab-made relative of allopregnanolone, a steroid the brain makes from progesterone.
It has no studied role in appearance. Its place on the wiki reflects interest in neurosteroids for mood, stress and sleep.
How it works: It enhances the inhibitory action of GABA at GABA-A receptors through a neurosteroid binding site. The label says the exact way this helps in postpartum depression is not fully understood.
Risks and caveats: The label has a boxed warning for impaired driving and lists sleepiness, dizziness and fatigue as common effects. It also warns about suicidal thoughts and possible fetal harm. It is prescription-only and a US Schedule IV controlled substance.
deepLead:
Zuranolone (brand name Zurzuvae) is an oral neuroactive steroid that acts as a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors. It is a synthetic analog of the body's own neurosteroid allopregnanolone and was developed by Sage Therapeutics with Biogen. The US FDA approved it in August 2023 for postpartum depression in adults, a 14-day oral course positioned as an alternative to intravenous brexanolone.
Zuranolone has no approved or studied use for appearance. It appears on the wiki as a recovery-category neurosteroid, in the context of community interest in mood, anxiety and sleep. Its US label carries a boxed warning about impaired driving and other hazardous activities, and it is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.
In published phase 3 trials in postpartum depression, patients given zuranolone showed greater reductions in depression scores than placebo at day 15. For major depressive disorder, the FDA issued a complete response letter citing insufficient evidence of effectiveness, while Japan approved it for depression in 2026.

name: Allopregnanolone

angle.text: Allopregnanolone is a natural progesterone-derived neurosteroid discussed in stress and sleep circles for its calming action on the brain. Interest in looks is indirect, via stress and rest; it has been studied for postpartum depression and not for appearance.

summary: Natural progesterone-derived neurosteroid behind the postpartum-depression drug brexanolone; no studied appearance use.
note: Poor oral bioavailability; approved form was an IV infusion since withdrawn from the US market.
currentQuick:
Allopregnanolone is a calming steroid made in the brain from progesterone. Its levels rise in pregnancy and drop after birth.
A synthetic IV version, brexanolone, was approved in 2019 for postpartum depression. Other uses remain in early trials, and no appearance use has been studied.
How it works: It boosts the effect of GABA at GABA-A receptors by binding to neurosteroid sites on the receptor, increasing inhibitory signalling.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects of the infused drug include sedation, dizziness, headache and dry mouth, with monitoring required. It is a controlled substance in the US, and is not available as a simple oral product because of low bioavailability.
deepLead:
Allopregnanolone (3alpha-hydroxy-5alpha-pregnan-20-one) is a neurosteroid the body makes from progesterone. It is a potent positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, the main inhibitory receptors in the brain. Its levels rise in stress, the luteal phase and pregnancy, and fall after delivery.
Its intravenous form, brexanolone, was approved by the US FDA in March 2019 for postpartum depression, the first neurosteroid approved; it was later withdrawn from the US market. Oral analogs such as zuranolone followed.
Allopregnanolone has no studied appearance use. Registered early-phase trials explore its use in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, traumatic brain injury and alcohol craving.

name: Kava (kavalactones)

angle.text: Users take kava to unwind, ease anxiety and sleep better, with the idea that lower stress shows in a more relaxed, rested face. Small trials have looked at anxiety, while appearance outcomes have not been studied.

summary: Pacific root drink and supplement for relaxation; small anxiety signal in trials, with a history of liver-safety bans.
note: Liver-injury reports led to bans in several countries; legal status varies.
currentQuick:
Kava is a traditional Pacific root drink, now also sold as capsules and extracts, used for relaxation and stress.
Trials suggest a small anxiety benefit, but some health bodies say the evidence is insufficient. It has no studied role in appearance.
How it works: Kavalactones are thought to act on GABA-A and several other receptors and channels, though the exact mechanism is not well established.
Risks and caveats: Reports of rare severe liver injury in the early 2000s led to restrictions, with regulators and the WHO distinguishing water-based traditional kava from solvent extracts. It also interacts with alcohol and some drugs, and its legal status varies by country.
deepLead:
Kava is a drink and extract made from the roots of Piper methysticum, a plant domesticated in the Pacific Islands, where it is used socially and ceremonially. Its main active constituents are kavalactones, of which six account for most of its pharmacological activity. In supplement form, it is used for anxiety, stress and sleep.
In vitro work indicates kavalactones act on GABA-A, dopamine and other receptors, though the precise mechanism is not fully understood. A 2003 systematic review reported a small anxiety benefit over placebo, while some health bodies conclude the evidence does not support effectiveness for generalized anxiety disorder.
Kava drew regulatory attention in the early 2000s after reports of liver injury linked to extracts, leading to bans or restrictions in several countries; several have since been revised. It has no studied appearance use and appears as a recovery-category herb.

name: Lavender oil capsules (Silexan)

angle.text: Silexan is taken as a calming supplement, and users in recovery-focused circles pair it with better sleep and lower stress for a more rested look. Placebo-controlled trials cover anxiety; appearance use is untested.

summary: Standardized oral lavender oil sold for anxiety; some placebo-controlled data, no appearance use.
note: Essential oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity, especially by children.
currentQuick:
Silexan is a capsule containing a standardized lavender oil, taken for anxiety and restlessness.
Controlled trials report reduced anxiety, though the NCCIH says oral effectiveness is not established. It has no studied appearance use.
How it works: Linalool and linalyl acetate are the main constituents. How the oral product acts is not settled in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Pure lavender oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity, with poisonings reported mostly in children. Topical oil can cause contact dermatitis, and interactions with some drugs have been noted.
deepLead:
Silexan is a standardized oral lavender oil preparation sold as capsules for anxiety and restlessness. It is made from Lavandula angustifolia flowers and marketed in Germany as a medicine and in the US as a supplement (CalmAid), according to a reference page.
Placebo-controlled trials of a daily oral dose reported reduced anxiety symptoms, and a 2010 trial compared it with lorazepam. The NCCIH states that the effectiveness of oral lavender for anxiety is not established. Lavender oil is also used in aromatherapy, perfumery and cosmetics, where its constituents include linalool and linalyl acetate.
Silexan has no studied appearance use. It is a recovery-category compound for anxiety and sleep. Lavender oil is toxic if swallowed in large amounts, especially for children.

name: Hops extract

angle.text: Hops extract is included in sleep blends, often with valerian or chamomile, by people seeking deeper sleep and a more rested appearance. Human evidence for its sedative effect is limited, and appearance use is unstudied.

summary: Beer-flavoring flower sold in sleep supplements; human sedative evidence is limited and appearance use is unstudied.
note: Phytoestrogen content (8-prenylnaringenin) noted in references.
currentQuick:
Hops are the flowers used in brewing, and extracts are sold for sleep and relaxation, often in blends.
Reference pages say human evidence for a sedative effect is limited. No appearance use has been studied.
How it works: Resin acids and flavonoids such as xanthohumol are the key compounds; one, 8-prenylnaringenin, is a potent phytoestrogen. How hops might affect sleep is not established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Hops are generally considered safe; contact dermatitis is reported in harvest workers. The phytoestrogen content is of research interest.
deepLead:
Hops are the cone-shaped flowers of the female Humulus lupulus plant, best known for flavoring beer. Extracts are also sold in sleep and relaxation supplements, often alongside valerian or chamomile.
Hops contain resins (alpha and beta acids), essential oils and polyphenols including the flavonoid xanthohumol and the phytoestrogen 8-prenylnaringenin. Reference pages report that evidence for sedative effects in humans is limited.
Hops extract has no studied appearance use; it is a recovery-category sleep herb. Few sources document community discussion.

name: Propranolol

chain: Claimed IGF-1 and BMP-2 bone signaling
angle.text: Forum posters take propranolol to calm physical anxiety symptoms before social situations, and some promote a theory that it stimulates bone growth and improves facial structure. The anxiety use is established medically; the bone-growth idea is untested in humans.

summary: Prescription beta blocker used off-label for performance anxiety; the forum bone-growth theory is untested in humans.
note: Abrupt discontinuation can worsen angina; contraindicated in asthma and heart block.
currentQuick:
Propranolol is a long-established prescription beta blocker for blood pressure, heart rhythm, migraine prevention and tremor. It is also used off-label to ease the physical symptoms of performance anxiety.
Forum users discuss it for social anxiety and, in some threads, bone growth; the bone claim comes from cell and animal data and has not been studied in people.
How it works: It blocks beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, blunting the effects of adrenaline on heart rate and tremor.
Risks and caveats: Common effects include fatigue, slow heart rate and nausea; it can worsen asthma, and abrupt stopping is warned against. It is prescription-only in most countries.
deepLead:
Propranolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker developed by Scottish pharmacologist James Black in the 1960s, patented in 1962 and first marketed as Inderal in 1965. It is prescribed for hypertension, angina, arrhythmias, migraine prevention, essential tremor and infantile hemangioma.
It is also used off-label for situational and performance anxiety, where it reduces physical symptoms such as tremor and racing heartbeat. A 2025 meta-analysis reported no benefit over placebo or benzodiazepines for social phobia or panic disorder, though evidence quality was limited.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed for social anxiety and, in some threads, for claimed bone or growth effects, which the cited preclinical research does not establish in humans. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Australia.

name: Tianeptine

angle.text: Tianeptine is an antidepressant that appears in gray-market stress and mood stacks, where users want less stress and more energy for daily life. Its link to looks is indirect via mood; it has been studied for depression, not appearance.

summary: A French antidepressant with opioid-receptor activity that shows up in gray-market supplements; nothing ties it to looks.
note: Mu-opioid agonist with documented dependence, withdrawal and overdose reports; FDA has warned about supplement products.
currentQuick:
Tianeptine is an antidepressant approved in France and some other countries. It is not FDA-approved but has been sold in the US as a supplement.
It appears in looksmaxxing spaces as a mood or focus aid. No study has examined it for any appearance outcome.
How it works: It acts as a mu-opioid receptor agonist and appears to modulate glutamate signalling and neuroplasticity.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks include dependence, opioid-like withdrawal, overdose and adulterated products. The FDA has issued warnings and several US states have scheduled it.
deepLead:
Tianeptine is an antidepressant sold under brand names such as Stablon and Coaxil in France and several other countries, where it is approved for major depressive disorder. It is not approved in the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia or by the US FDA. It was developed in the 1960s and introduced in France in 1983.
Its pharmacology differs from that of typical antidepressants. It acts as an agonist at the mu-opioid receptor and also appears to affect glutamate signalling and neuroplasticity. At high doses it can produce opioid-like effects, and prolonged high-dose use has been associated with dependence and withdrawal.
In the United States it has been sold online and in some retail outlets as a dietary supplement, and the FDA has issued warnings about recreational use and about products found to contain undeclared tianeptine. On appearance-focused forums it is mentioned mainly in the context of mood and focus rather than looks, and no studies have examined it for any appearance outcome.

name: Tiratricol (Triac)

angle.text: Tiratricol was once sold as a fat-burner because thyroid-hormone analogues raise metabolic rate, which people link to leanness. It is approved today for a rare genetic disorder; its use for fat loss rests on case reports and anecdote rather than trials.

summary: A thyroid-hormone analogue now approved for a rare genetic disorder, once sold as a fat-burner with case reports of thyroid dysfunction.
note: US label carries a boxed warning against use for obesity or weight loss.
currentQuick:
Tiratricol is a synthetic thyroid hormone analogue. It is approved for peripheral thyrotoxicosis in MCT8 deficiency, a rare genetic condition.
In the early 2000s it was sold in OTC fat-loss supplements. No trial has tested it for weight loss.
How it works: It activates thyroid hormone receptors and can enter cells without the MCT8 transporter.
Risks and caveats: Case reports describe hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and periodic paralysis from supplement use. The label warns against use for obesity or weight loss.
deepLead:
Tiratricol, also called Triac or triiodothyroacetic acid, is a synthetic thyroid hormone analogue that binds thyroid hormone receptors. It is approved in the EU and, according to a US prescribing label, in the United States as Emcitate for peripheral thyrotoxicosis in people with MCT8 deficiency (Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome).
Outside that use, tiratricol was sold in the early 2000s in over-the-counter fat-loss supplements, and case reports describe hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and periodic paralysis in users. The US label carries a boxed warning that thyroid hormones should not be used for obesity or weight loss.
No clinical trial has tested tiratricol as a weight-loss or appearance treatment.

name: Levothyroxine (T4)

angle.text: Some users aim to correct low-normal thyroid levels with levothyroxine to feel better, hold less water and fat, and look leaner. It is the standard treatment for hypothyroidism; appearance gains in people with normal thyroid function have not been studied.

summary: The standard hypothyroidism drug, which carries a boxed warning against use for weight loss.
note: Boxed warning: not for obesity or weight loss; excess doses can cause serious cardiac effects.
currentQuick:
Levothyroxine is synthetic T4, prescribed for hypothyroidism and some thyroid cancers.
It is sometimes discussed on forums in connection with weight and hormone optimisation, though no trial supports an appearance use in people with normal thyroid function.
How it works: It is converted to T3, which binds thyroid hormone receptors and regulates gene transcription and metabolism.
Risks and caveats: Overdose causes hyperthyroid symptoms including arrhythmia and bone loss. The label warns against use for weight loss, and it is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Levothyroxine is a synthetic form of thyroxine (T4), the main hormone made by the thyroid gland. It is the standard replacement therapy for hypothyroidism and is also used to suppress TSH in some thyroid cancers.
Because excess thyroid hormone causes weight loss, levothyroxine has been misused for slimming. The US label carries a boxed warning that it should not be used to treat obesity or for weight loss, stating that doses within normal replacement ranges are ineffective for weight reduction in euthyroid patients and larger doses may cause serious toxicity.
On looksmaxxing forums it is discussed mainly by people who suspect or have borderline thyroid abnormalities, sometimes alongside growth hormone. No trials have examined it as an appearance treatment in people with normal thyroid function.
